title: South Korea's Staggering Drop in Working Hours

scenes.narration: Did you know South Korean workers logged 2,919 hours per year back in 1970?

visual.text: South Korea's Staggering Drop in Working Hours

scenes.narration: In 1970, South Korea recorded one of the most intense work schedules in the world.
But as industrialization matured and living standards rose, annual working hours dropped by 35% to 1,910 hours in 2023.
Meanwhile, workers in the United States logged 1,789 hours in 2023, while the United Kingdom recorded 1,523 hours.

title: How Germany Built the Shortest Work Year

scenes.narration: How did Germany become the lowest-working nation in the world at just 1,335 hours per year?

visual.text: How Germany Built the Shortest Work Year

scenes.narration: Back in 1970, German workers put in 1,972 hours annually.
Over the next half-century, rising productivity and strong labor policies drove a 32% reduction in working hours.
By contrast, United Kingdom workers logged 1,523 hours in 2023, while American workers recorded 1,789 hours.
Germany shows how advanced economies turned economic efficiency into free time.

title: Does National Wealth Actually Buy Free Time?

scenes.narration: Does higher national wealth actually guarantee fewer working hours for citizens?

visual.text: Does National Wealth Actually Buy Free Time?

scenes.narration: Data across 126 nations reveals an inverse relationship, with GDP per person and work hours moving in opposite directions at a correlation of -0.40.
The United States boasts a GDP per person of $74,352 while workers log 1,789 hours per year.
Germany reaches $63,140 per person, yet its workers put in just 1,335 hours.
While wealth enables shorter schedules, local institutional norms set the pace of life.
